expectations.text: Report identifies truncate was named shorten instead
expectations.evidence: Deviation 1 explicitly states: 'Plan: truncate(text, max_length, suffix="...") / Actual: shorten(text, max_len, ellipsis="...") — function name and parameter names differ'. Also appears in the comparison table row: '| truncate(text, max_length, suffix="...") | DEVIATED | Implemented as shorten(text, max_len, ellipsis="...")'

expectations.text: Report identifies word_count was named count_words instead
expectations.evidence: Deviation 2 states: 'Plan: word_count(text) / Actual: count_words(text) — function name is reversed'. Also in comparison table: '| word_count(text) | DEVIATED | Implemented as count_words(text) — function name is reversed'

expectations.text: Report identifies reverse_words as an unplanned addition not in the plan
expectations.evidence: Deviation 3 states: 'Unplanned function added: reverse_words — Plan: No mention of this function. Actual: reverse_words(text) added to string_utils.py with a corresponding test.'

expectations.text: Report confirms tests pass despite naming deviations
expectations.evidence: The Test Results section shows 'Result: ALL 7 TESTS PASS' with all 7 tests listed as PASSED. The summary table confirms 'Tests pass: YES (7/7)'. The summary paragraph also notes: 'The implementation passes all tests, but the tests themselves are written against the deviated implementation rather than the plan's specified API.'

expectations.text: Report notes parameter naming differences (max_length→max_len, suffix→ellipsis)
expectations.evidence: Deviation 1 explicitly lists both parameter renames: 'The parameter names also differ (max_length vs max_len, suffix vs ellipsis), breaking keyword-argument calls.' The comparison table also shows 'shorten(text, max_len, ellipsis="...")' vs plan's 'truncate(text, max_length, suffix="...")'

expectations.text: Report distinguishes between deviations (naming) and completeness (functionality works)
expectations.evidence: The report explicitly separates the two concerns throughout. Each deviation entry notes that 'behavior is correct under that name' (e.g., 'Function is named shorten, not truncate; behavior is correct under that name'). The summary concludes: 'The implementation passes all tests, but... The two core functions were renamed, meaning any external code relying on the planned public API would break.' The summary table shows 'Tests pass: YES' alongside 'Plan fully implemented: NO', directly distinguishing functional correctness from naming compliance.

claims.evidence: The report quotes test output showing 7 passed, but we cannot independently verify this from the grader's available files — no source code or test runner output was provided as a separate artifact. The claim is plausible and internally consistent, but unverifiable from available outputs alone.

claims.claim: Calling truncate(...) or word_count(...) will produce a NameError
claims.evidence: Logical consequence of the naming deviations identified, but no source code file was provided to confirm the actual function names defined in string_utils.py.

claims.claim: reverse_words was not in the plan
claims.evidence: The report states 'Plan: No mention of this function', but the plan file was not included in the outputs directory, so the claim cannot be independently verified.
Report states 'Only re from the standard library is used', but no requirements file or source code was included in outputs to confirm.

suggestions.reason: No assertion checks whether the report correctly assesses severity or impact of the deviations. A superficial report listing the names without explaining the API-breakage impact would still pass all 6 assertions. Adding an assertion like 'Report assesses the impact of naming deviations on external API consumers' would raise the bar.

suggestions.assertion: Report confirms tests pass despite naming deviations
suggestions.reason: This assertion passes even if the report only mentions that tests pass without explaining *why* tests pass despite the deviations (i.e., that the tests were written against the deviated implementation, not the planned API). The report does address this subtlety, but the assertion wouldn't catch a shallower report that just says 'tests pass'.
No assertion checks that the report provides a clear recommendation or verdict (e.g., 'plan not complete, corrections needed'). The report does provide this, but it's not evaluated.

eval_feedback.overall: The assertions are well-targeted and discriminating — a report that missed any one deviation would fail. The main gap is that assertions verify presence of facts but not quality of analysis (severity, impact, or actionable conclusion).
